headline: GitLab presents itself as a fully remote, mission-driven workplace where transparency, inclusion, and the freedom to contribute from anywhere define the culture.
identity: GitLab has consistently valued all-remote autonomy, universal contribution ('everyone can contribute'), transparency, and diversity/inclusion across its careers copy from 2015 to the present. The altruism and inclusion language started near the bottom of the peer range in 2015–2017 (zscores around -1.2 to -1.4) and climbed steadily to well above average by 2022–2026 (zscores above 1.0), reflecting a deliberate expansion of mission-oriented and belonging-focused messaging. The one notable wavering: the 2023 careers page was strikingly thin — only 6 content chunks versus 34–67 in surrounding years — causing inclusion, performance, wellbeing, and meritocracy scores to collapse to their lowest zscores in the dataset (as low as -2.57), suggesting a significant page redesign or content gap that year rather than a sustained retreat.
fit: You might be a good fit if you are comfortable working asynchronously across time zones, motivated by a stated mission that 'everyone can contribute,' and drawn to a culture that explicitly frames results over hours spent — the copy consistently reaches for people who want autonomy, cross-functional impact from day one, and a transparent, handbook-first operating style.

sections.heading: From Scrappy Remote Startup to Inclusion-Forward Mission Company
sections.body:
In 2015–2017, the careers copy was sparse (2–3 chunks, flagged thin) and focused almost entirely on productivity and independence: 'joining a very productive, ambitious team, where independence is both valued and required.' Diversity language was absent; all DEI registers were coded 'absent' for those years.

The shift began in 2018, when a 'Join a diverse, global team' section appeared for the first time, introducing specific language about inclusive interviewing panels, transgender medical benefits listed publicly, and sponsorship of diversity-in-tech events. The inclusion zscore jumped from -0.97 (2016) to +0.80 (2018). By 2020–2021, the copy added 'belonging' to the standard 'diversity and inclusion' phrase and named specific Team Member Resource Groups (GitLab Pride, GitLab Women, GitLab Minorities in Tech).

By 2022, the altruism zscore reached +1.23 and the page carried a dedicated 'Diversity & Inclusion' section stating 'Diversity, Inclusion, & Belonging is woven into our values and everything we do.' The 2025–2026 copy reframes the section heading as 'Inclusion & Belonging' and adds 'We create spaces where everyone belongs,' the highest-scoring inclusion sentence in the dataset (0.617).

sections.heading: The All-Remote Identity: Central, Then Quieter
sections.body:
Remote work is the most persistent structural theme across all years. From 2015's 'remote only company' to 2021's explicit claim of being 'one of the world's largest all-remote companies' and a 'prolific inventor of remote best practices,' the copy leaned hard into remote as a competitive differentiator. The techno-optimism score peaked in 2021 (zscore +1.45), driven by quotes like 'In the future, companies who make digital products are going to be much more all-remote' and 'I think it's going to be the future.'

After 2021, techno-optimism around remote work faded. By 2025 the techno-optimism zscore dropped to -2.12 — the lowest in the dataset — and the 2026 copy quietly softened 'asynchronous' to 'asynchronous and synchronous working style,' a small but concrete signal that the all-remote absolutism of 2021 has been walked back in the language.

Wellbeing language followed a similar arc: it peaked in 2019 (zscore +1.59, with specific copy about flexible hours for caregivers and adventurers) and again in 2022 (zscore +1.31, with personal 'Moments that Matter' employee stories about kids, skiing, and repatriation), then fell sharply in 2023 and has not fully recovered.

sections.heading: The 2023 Anomaly and What Came After
sections.body:
The 2023 careers page is an outlier across every facet: only 6 content chunks, zscores of -2.57 (performance), -2.33 (meritocracy), -1.97 (mission_rights), -1.58 (wellbeing), and -1.97 (inclusion). The surviving quotes are mostly product-focused ('GitLab is the most comprehensive DevSecOps platform') and historical ('Anniversary of our first ever summit in Amsterdam'). This looks like a stripped-down or transitional page rather than a deliberate messaging shift, because 2024–2026 pages recovered most of the prior language.

From 2024 onward, the copy stabilized around a tighter set of recurring phrases: 'a world where everyone can contribute,' 'show up as their full selves,' 'transparent environment where all team members feel their voices are heard,' and — new in 2025–2026 — 'AI-powered DevSecOps platform' and 'ship software at the speed of imagination.' The AI framing is the clearest new identity signal in recent copy, though it appears only in a few sentences and has not yet displaced the values-and-belonging language that dominates the page.
